The ancient poets for the most part give Bacchus horns. It is therefore quite strange, says Spence, that one so rarely sees these horns on his statues. <note>a)</note> He hits upon this, he hits upon another cause, upon the ignorance of the antiquarians, upon the smallness of the horns themselves, which might have hidden themselves among the grapes and ivy leaves, the constant headgear of the god. He winds himself around the true cause without suspecting it. The horns of Bacchus were not natural horns, as they were on the fauns and satyrs. They were an ornament for the forehead that he could put on and take off.

> When you stand there without horns,
> Your head is maidenly: <note>original: "Tibi, cum sine cornibus adstas / Virgineum caput est"</note>

<margin>a) Polymetis Dial. IX. p. 129.</margin>

<summary>Lessing critiques Spence's failure to recognize that poetry and painting possess distinct aesthetic boundaries, using the example of Bacchus's horns to illustrate how poets and artists employ different conventions.</summary>

of a few hours more, as we call them, whitish, they finally, after the fourth or the sixth day, deposit everything, remaining pure and clear: can their resistance to penetration stop those impalpable and insensible atoms of sand, which, because of their minimal force, consume six days to descend the space of half a braccio <note>A unit of length, roughly equivalent to an arm's length or half a meter.</note>? What then is this thickness of water, with which it resists division? What, upon our faith, could it be, if we (as I have also said above), with all diligence attempting to reduce a material so similar in gravity to water that, forming it even into a very wide sheet, it remains suspended, as we say, between the two waters; it is impossible to achieve this, although we bring ourselves to such a similarity of equilibrium that as much lead, as is the fourth part of a grain of millet, added to said very wide sheet, which in air will weigh four or six pounds, leads it to the bottom, and removed, it comes to the surface of the water? I cannot see (if what I say is true, as it is most true) what minimal virtue and force one would have to be able to find or imagine, of which the resistance of water to being divided and pulled apart would not be less, from which, by necessity, it is concluded that it is nothing: because if it were of some sensible power, some wide sheet could be found or composed of material similar in gravity to water, which not only would stop between the two waters, but could not, without notable force, be lowered or raised. We could likewise gather the same truth from another experiment, showing how water in the same way yields also to transversal division, because, if in still and stagnant water we place any very large mass, which does not go to the bottom, pulling it with a single hair of a woman, we will move it from place to place, without any contrast, and let its shape be whatever one wishes, such that it embraces a great space of water, as a large beam would do, moved crosswise. Perhaps someone could oppose me, saying that if the resistance of water to being divided were, as I affirm, nothing, ships should not need so much force of oars or sails to be pushed from place to place in the calm sea or in stagnant lakes. To whoever made such objections, I would respond that water does not contrast or resist division simply, but rather it does resist being divided quickly, and with so much greater resistance as the speed is greater: and the cause of such resistance does not depend on thickness or anything else that absolutely contrasts with division, but

<summary>Galileo argues that water offers no inherent resistance to objects passing through it, as evidenced by fine sand settling and the impossibility of perfectly suspending an object through water's "thickness." He notes that water's resistance is a product of speed rather than internal tenacity.</summary>
<keywords>water, resistance, division, gravity, equilibrium, motion, speed</keywords>

through the means with God in this unity, we are received by the Holy Spirit; <margin>How noble this unity is.</margin> and we receive the Holy Spirit and the Father and the Son and the divine nature all together, for one cannot divide God. And the fruition-giving inclination of the spirit, which seeks rest in God above all likeness, attains and possesses supernaturally in its essential being all that the spirit ever received naturally therein. All good people have this, but how that is, remains hidden from them all their life, unless they are inward and empty of all creatures and enlightened with spiritual understanding. In the very <margin>As soon as a person turns from sin, they are received by God.</margin> moment that a person turns away from sin, they are received by God in the essential unity of themselves, in that highest part of their spirit, so that they may rest in God now and always. And they receive grace and a likeness of God in the faculty of their powers, so that they always grow and increase in virtues. And as long as that likeness exists in <term>charity</term> <gloss>divine love</gloss> and in virtues, so the unity exists in rest, and it cannot be lost except through mortal sin.

<summary>This page explains that the soul is received into essential unity with God at the moment of turning away from sin, a state characterized by a supernatural rest that persists as long as the soul remains in charity and virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Holy Spirit, divine nature, fruition-giving inclination, essential unity, mortal sin, charity, spiritual growth</keywords>

I say, therefore, that in the first method, which is that festive narration, no art is needed, because nature itself creates and forms men apt to narrate pleasantly, and gives them the face, the gestures, the voice, and the words appropriate to imitate what they wish. In the other method of witticisms, what can art do? Since that witty remark must have come forth and hit the mark before it appears that he who says it could have been able to think about it; otherwise it is cold and lacks goodness. Therefore, I estimate that the whole thing is a work of wit and nature.

Then M. Pietro Bembo replied to the words and said, "The Lord Prefect does not deny you what you say, that is, that nature and talent do not have the primary roles, especially regarding invention, but it is certain that in the soul of each person, let a man be of as good a talent as he can be, good and bad concepts are born; more or less, but judgment later, and art, files and corrects them, and makes a selection of the good ones and rejects the bad ones." Therefore, leaving aside what pertains to talent, explain to us what consists of art, that is, regarding <term>facetie</term> <gloss>witty remarks</gloss> and <term>motti</term> <gloss>jokes/quips</gloss> that induce laughter, which ones are suitable for the Courtier and which ones are not, and in what time and manner they should be used, for this is what the Lord Prefect asks of you.

Then M. Federico, also laughing, said, "There is no one here among us to whom I do not yield in every thing, and especially in being witty, except if perhaps the sillinesses, which often make others laugh more than beautiful sayings, were not themselves also accepted as witty remarks." And so, turning to Count Lodovico and to M. Bernardo Bibiena, he said, "Here are the masters of this."

<summary>The interlocutors continue to debate whether wit is a natural talent or a refined art. M. Pietro Bembo argues that while talent is primary, judgment and art are necessary to refine and select appropriate witticisms for the courtier.</summary>

### CHAPTER LXVI.

**How the next day we sent messengers to the Caciques of Tlascala, begging them for peace, and what they did regarding this.**

After the battle I have recounted had passed, in which we captured the three principal Indians, our Captain Cortés sent them off, and with the two who were in our camp who had gone other times as messengers, he ordered them to tell the Caciques of Tlascala that we begged them to come at once in peace, and to grant us passage through their land to go to Mexico, as we had sent to tell them other times: and that if they do not come now, we will kill all their people, and because we love them much, and wish to have them as brothers, we would not want to anger them, if they had not given cause for it, and many flatteries were spoken to them to attract them to our friendship: and those messengers went willingly at once to the capital of Tlascala, and delivered their embassy to all the Caciques, already named by me: whom they found gathered with many other elders and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and they were very sad, both from the poor success of the war, and from the death of the Captains, their relatives or children, who died in the battles, and it is said that they did not want to listen to them willingly; and what they agreed upon regarding this was that they immediately ordered the summoning of all the diviners and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and others who cast lots, whom they call <term>Tacalnagual</term> <gloss>sorcerers/fortune-tellers</gloss>, who are like wizards, and they told them to look through their divinations and spells and lots, to see what kind of people we were, and if we could be defeated by giving us battle by day and by night continuously, and also to know if we were <term>Teules</term> <gloss>gods or demons</gloss>, just as those from Cempoal said, which I have already said other times are evil things like demons, and what things we ate, and to look at all this with great diligence: and after the diviners and wizards and many <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss> gathered, and their divinations made, and their lots cast, and everything they were accustomed to doing; it seems they said that in the lots they found that we were men of bone and flesh, and that we ate chickens, and dogs, and bread, and fruit when we had it, and that we did not eat the flesh of Indians, nor the hearts of those we killed, because, as it appeared, the friendly Indians we brought from Cempoal made them believe that we were <term>Teules</term> <gloss>gods or demons</gloss>, and that the cannons threw lightning like that which falls from the sky, and that the greyhound was a tiger or a lion, and that the horses were for lancing the Indians when we wanted to kill them; and they told them many other childish things. And let us return to the <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and the worst of all that their <term>Papas</term> and diviners told them was that we could not be defeated by day, only by night, because as it grew dark our strength left us: and the wizards told them more, that we were brave, and that we possessed all these virtues by day until the Sun set, and once it grew dark we had no strength at all. And when the Caciques heard that, and held it to be very certain, they sent to tell their Captain General Xicotenga to come at once with haste one night with great forces to give us battle. He, as he learned this, gathered about ten thousand Indians, the most valiant he had, and came to our camp, and from three directions began to give us a volley of arrows, and to throw spears with their spear-throwers of one and two prongs, and those with swords and clubs and great two-handed swords from another side, so that suddenly they felt certain that they would carry off some of us to sacrifice; and our Lord God provided better, that however secretly they came, they found us very prepared; because as they felt the great noise they made approaching, our field scouts and spies came to call to arms; and as we were so accustomed to sleeping shod, and our armor on, and the horses saddled and bridled, and all kinds of weapons very ready, we resisted them with the muskets and crossbows, and with sword thrusts they quickly turned their backs, and as it was level ground, and

<header>Description of Lima, city of the Kings.</header>

<margin>
Form of the city of Lima.
</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some are very beautiful with little towers and galleries. The marketplace is large, and the streets are wide, all running straight toward the market, from where one can also see into all the corners, and on both sides lies the flat country. Through most of these houses, channels flow out, bringing fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort to the citizens, who can through this water their orchards and vegetable gardens, which they have clean and pleasant. Also,

<margin>
Many water mills, with which they grind their corn.
</margin>
there are many water mills in this river, after the manner of our country, where they grind their corn. In short, very rich citizens live here, some of whom have 150,000 ducats. And from this city, ships sometimes sail worth 800,000 ducats, and some even worth a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high hill upon which a crucifix stands. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their beasts and their dovecotes, their vineyards (though no good grapes, due to the nature of the land), and beautiful gardens, full not only of all sorts of fruit of that land, but also

<margin>
Description of the fertility of the land.
</margin>
of Spanish fruits, such as figs, pomegranates, limes, lemons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar cane, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. And truly, to pass human life with joy, if there were not the scandals, disagreements, and wars there, this place is certainly one of the most beautiful in the entire world, for the climate there is so temperate that throughout the whole year there is no excessive heat or harmful cold. One has also never seen hunger or plague there, or any rain, or claps of thunder, or lightning from the heavens

<margin>
Why the city of the Kings obtained its name, and was built in the year 1535.
</margin>
struck: but on the contrary, always a bright, clear, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535. It is called the city of the Kings because the people were brought into it on the day of the Three Kings <note>Epiphany, January 6th</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish, which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as also meat and fruits of the trees and the earth as has been said, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. The four months when it is summer in Spain are winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist falls every day before noon, like a fog, though not unhealthy as it is with us: for those who have pain in the head, by washing themselves with this, find relief. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will increase daily in people and riches, even though for many years there were over 500 houses

<margin>
The breadth and length of the houses of Lima.
</margin>
and the city is built very widely, so that there could well be 2,000, for the streets are wide and the marketplace is large; each house has 80 feet of ground area and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors (for it is destroyed by worms within 2 or 3 years), the houses are built with only one story, yet still very

<margin>
Form of the houses
</margin>
costly and magnificent with many rooms, halls, and parlors, suitable for living and for housing strange guests. The walls are made of some materials which they bake together very thickly, and they fill them with earth. They cover their houses with painted mats or painted linen, around and above <column-break/> on the walls they make little bowers of foliage where they take shelter from the sun. They do not need to worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where Bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trugillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus Vetus, Guayaquil, Popaian, Carchi, S. Michael, S. Francisco. It has been said before that Peru is divided into three types of landscape: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Regarding the flat land by the seashore, we have treated that until now, beginning from the <term>Linea</term> <gloss>Equator</gloss> and C. Passao up to this point. It is also to be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima, but much further, the seacoast to the south is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places where for 10 miles of distance it neither thunders, lightens, nor rains, but beyond those 10 miles it does, or as much more or less as the mountain range lies from the sea. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but indeed 4 or 5 stagnant waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants support themselves with the water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which take their source from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, not from springs, which are few in the mountains. The distances of these rivers are partly described here before, lying 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from one another, though mostly 7 or 8, by which the traveling people regulate themselves, because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, a mile wide or sometimes wider, sometimes less, according to the situation of the land, there are different fertile trees and corn lands that are cultivated and sown by the people, which they can do throughout the whole year. Around these rivers also grow many kinds of wild trees, cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and irises, etc. And after the Spaniards have taken the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through some channels they lead from these rivers, which, because they run down quickly from high mountains, one can hardly cross without help, and many have drowned in them. Those who make their journey along the flat land keep generally so close to the seaside that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and it rains much, it is dangerous to travel there because of the swelling of the rivers one must cross, either with certain rafts they have for that purpose, or with a net that they fill tightly with gourds <note>original: "Cauwaerden"; likely referring to dry, buoyant squash gourds used as floats</note>, upon which the traveler must lie stretched out, and one of the Indians swims in front, pulling the net or the rafts with a rope, and another steering from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of foliage. The men wear shirts and cloths reaching to the knees and extending over them, and an uppermost garment like a mantle. The women wear a course <note>kirtle or tunic</note> of cotton according to the length of the body, and even though the fashion of the clothing is almost everywhere the same, there is nevertheless some difference in the ornamentation of the head: for some wear single cords, some braided ones, some of one type, others of various colors, and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, and all are distinguished according to the custom of the land.
